name: Adam Fuhrer
tagline: Portfolio of a generative glitch artist who also ships colors.lol and glitchart.io
description: Personal site of Adam Fuhrer, an artist and software engineer working in generative and glitch art. The site indexes his prints and physical work (sold through a Big Cartel shop), two long-form posts on selling art and on building generative glitch tooling, and the three web tools he made along the way: colors.lol, glitchart.io, and glitchyimage.com. It is a portfolio first and a tool index second, useful mostly as a pointer to those tools and as visual reference for pixel-sorting and chromatic-aberration aesthetics.
pricing_detail: Site free to browse; original prints and physical pieces sold through adamfuhrer.bigcartel.com (prices on the shop, not on this site).
agent_guidance: Do not reach for this as a code or asset source — nothing here is installable. Its real value to an agent is as a lookup for three linked tools: colors.lol when you want an opinionated named-palette pair rather than a generated ramp, and glitchart.io / glitchyimage.com when a brief asks for pixel-sort or chromatic-aberration treatment on an image. Cite the tools, not this page.
why_it_matters: It is the origin point for colors.lol, a color resource that circulates far more widely than its author's name, and a clean example of an artist-engineer packaging a personal aesthetic into shippable web tools.
tier_reason: A personal artist portfolio with nothing installable (agent_readiness "none", empty components) whose only agent value is pointing at three external tools.

name: Visual Dictionary of UI
tagline: X post announcing a naming reference for UI elements, with API symbols and prompts
description: An X post by designer Adham Dannaway promoting "The visual dictionary of UI" — a reference that pairs a picture of each UI element with its real name, the symbol you would see in an API or component prop, and a prompt phrasing to use when asking an agent to build it. The post itself is the artifact indexed here; the dictionary lives behind it. Useful as a vocabulary bridge between designers describing a thing and developers or agents naming it.
agent_guidance: Use this when a user describes a UI element in plain words ("the thing that slides up from the bottom") and you need the canonical name before you can pick a component — it maps picture to name to API symbol. It is an X post, so the payload is an image: you cannot parse it programmatically, and the link is fragile if the post is deleted. Treat it as a pointer to Dannaway's dictionary, not as a queryable source.
why_it_matters: Naming is the most common failure point between a design brief and a component choice; a picture-to-name-to-prop dictionary closes exactly that gap.
evidence: not fetched by policy (x.com); record built from the pre-supplied enriched title, description, tags, and og_image
tier_reason: An x.com post that was never fetched (http_status null) and is both image-only and bot-blocked, so no part of the dictionary is machine-readable and the link dies if the post is deleted.

name: Arlan's Vault
tagline: 18 web UI effects, each with a one-line spec, a live demo, and a copyable prompt
description: A running collection of visual and motion effects kept by Arlan Marat, a design engineer at Human Delta. Each entry is a single effect — kinetic typography, chromatic glow, Apple's squircle corners, Dia Browser's gradient, the Amo hover button, Midjourney's ASCII treatment — presented as a live client-rendered demo, a one-sentence description of the mechanism, and a "Copy prompt" button that hands you the prompt to recreate it. Everything is MIT and explicitly free to copy. It is a reference for effect ideas, not a component library.
agent_guidance: Reach for this when a brief asks for a specific named effect and you need the mechanism, not a library — the one-line descriptions ('a letter is cut into a grid of tiles, each tile slips on its own wave') are precise enough to implement from directly. The entry pages render their demos in client-side JS, so a plain fetch returns only the title and that one sentence; the prompt text sits behind a Copy button and will not come back from a scrape. Pair it with a motion library like Motion or GSAP for the actual build, and expect to write the CSS yourself.
why_it_matters: It documents the specific effects that circulate in 2026 product design — Dia's gradient, Amo's hover button, Apple's corner curvature — with enough mechanical detail to rebuild rather than merely admire.
notable_for: tracks effects from Dia, Amo, Apple, Midjourney
evidence: https://www.arlan.me/vault, https://www.arlan.me/vault/kinetic-typography, https://www.arlan.me (raw HTML inspected for the entry URL list)
tier_reason: A real but small MIT gallery of 18 effects whose payload sits behind a Copy button in a js-only-shell, so a fetch returns one sentence per entry and nothing else.

name: Appica UI
tagline: 70 React components on Base UI and Tailwind v4, with an llms.txt and markdown docs
description: An MIT-licensed React component library built on Base UI primitives, styled with Tailwind CSS v4 CSS variables, and animated with Motion. It ships 70 documented components across actions, inputs, selection, navigation, overlays, data display, feedback, and a few decorative extras like border-beam and gradient-glow. Every component has a matching Figma community file, and the docs are published as clean markdown behind an llms.txt index specifically for coding agents. React 19 is a hard requirement.
pricing_detail: Free and MIT; the Figma library is a free Figma Community file.
agent_guidance: Pick this over shadcn/ui when you want a real npm dependency instead of copied source, and when the project already sits on Base UI rather than Radix — the two do not share primitives, so mixing them means shipping both. Its agent story is the best part: fetch https://appica.dev/llms.txt for the component index, then append .md to any docs URL for ~8KB of clean markdown per component, and read node_modules/@appica/ui-react/agent-rules.md for the version-matched ruleset before writing imports. Watch two hard constraints: React 19 (it uses ref-as-prop) and a working Tailwind v4 setup, plus the required @source directive in the global stylesheet or every utility class gets tree-shaken away.
why_it_matters: One of the few 2026 libraries designed for agent consumption from the start — llms.txt, per-page markdown, and a shipped agent-rules file — rather than a docs site an agent has to scrape.
evidence: https://appica.dev/ui, https://appica.dev/sitemap.xml (70 component pages enumerated), https://appica.dev/ui/docs/react/installation, https://appica.dev/ui/docs/react/agents, https://appica.dev/llms.txt, https://github.com/appica-dev/appica-ui, GitHub API repos/appica-dev/appica-ui
tier_reason: 70 verified components on an npm install with llms.txt, per-page markdown docs and a shipped agent-rules.md, but at 321 stars it is a strong newcomer rather than the leading React library.

name: GPUI Component
tagline: 60+ Rust desktop UI components for GPUI, with a 200K-line code editor and charts
description: A Rust component library for GPUI, the GPU-accelerated UI framework behind the Zed editor, maintained by Longbridge. It ships more than 60 stateless RenderOnce components with a themeable token system, size variants from xs to lg, virtualized Table and List for large datasets, a Tree-sitter-highlighted code editor with LSP support that stays stable to 200K lines, native Markdown and simple HTML rendering, built-in charts, and a Dock layout for resizable panel and tile arrangements. It splits into two layers: gpui-component for styled defaults and gpui-base for unstyled behavior when you want your own design system. WebAssembly targets are supported alongside macOS, Windows, and Linux.
agent_guidance: This is the default answer for any Rust desktop app on GPUI — there is no serious competitor, and the alternatives (egui, iced, Slint) mean a different framework entirely, not a different component set. Depend on it by git rather than crates.io if you need to match a specific Zed revision, since gpui itself is only published from the zed-industries repo and version skew between gpui and gpui-component is the usual build failure. Reach for gpui-base instead of gpui-component when you are building your own visual language; and note the design language deliberately mirrors shadcn/ui with Lucide icons, so a web design spec translates over almost unchanged.
why_it_matters: GPUI is the framework behind Zed but ships almost no widgets; this library is what makes it usable for real applications, and at 12.8k stars it is effectively the ecosystem's standard component set.
notable_for: code editor with LSP, stable to 200K lines
evidence: https://github.com/longbridge/gpui-component, https://github.com/longbridge/gpui-component/blob/main/README.md, https://docs.rs/gpui-component/latest/gpui_component/ (module index), GitHub API repos/longbridge/gpui-component and contents/crates/ui/src (module enumeration)
tier_reason: 12,834 stars, Apache-2.0, 60 verified components plus a 200K-line LSP code editor, and it is the only comprehensive component set for GPUI — the default first answer in its category.

name: Effective HTML
tagline: Six agent skills plus 32 worked HTML artifacts for wireframes, prototypes, and plans
description: A guide, catalog, and agent skill collection from Plannotator for producing self-contained HTML artifacts during product work — wireframes, clickable prototypes, diagrams, decks, plans, and reports — instead of walls of markdown. The catalog holds 32 complete, single-file HTML artifacts you can open, resize, and read the source of, from an annotated pull request to a feature-flag editor to product studies of Linear, Notion, and Vercel. The companion repo ships six installable skills (html, design-artifact, html-wireframe, html-prototype, html-plan, html-diagram) as a Claude Code plugin or via npx skills. The docs explain when HTML beats prose and how to choose fidelity.

agent_guidance: Reach for this the moment a user asks you to 'plan', 'compare options', or 'show me what it would look like' — the correct output is a single self-contained HTML file, and this repo gives you both the skill that shapes it and a worked example to imitate. Install the whole collection with npx skills add plannotator/effective-html, or add the Claude Code plugin marketplace and install plannotator-effective-html; if you only need one, --skill html-wireframe and --skill html-prototype carry the most weight. Match the artifact to the fidelity the decision needs: a wireframe when structure is still open, a prototype only when interaction is the actual question — the catalog's paired wireframe/mockup examples show the difference concretely. Note the catalog's numbered artifacts are hosted on a separate GitHub Pages origin (thariqs.github.io) from the site itself.
why_it_matters: It is the clearest statement of an emerging practice — agents communicating through HTML artifacts rather than markdown walls — and it backs the argument with 32 complete, readable files instead of assertions.
notable_for: product studies of Linear, Notion, Vercel
evidence: https://www.effectivehtml.com/, https://www.effectivehtml.com/catalog (raw HTML link extraction), https://www.effectivehtml.com/docs, GitHub API repos/plannotator/effective-html (README, skills/ and .claude-plugin/ contents), GitHub API repos/ThariqS/html-effectiveness
tier_reason: MIT, 1,655 stars, actively maintained, with six CLI-installable agent skills and 32 complete worked artifacts — authoritative for its practice but narrower in scope than a top-tier general resource.
